headline: A warm, breezy Tuesday gives way to a high-moisture Kentucky rain band Wednesday, while the Upstate stays unsettled into Thursday
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: A tightening gradient between Mid-Atlantic high pressure and a Plains upper low produces a warm, breezy Tuesday. Tonight, a 55–65 kt low-level jet transports anomalously deep moisture into Kentucky ahead of an occluding front. Widespread rain, embedded thunder and gusty showers cross Central Kentucky Wednesday. Weak instability limits the broader severe risk despite strong shear, while deep warm-cloud depth and flow parallel to the front support efficient or briefly training rainfall. Residual drizzle ends Wednesday night before transient drying Thursday.
kentucky.currentConditions: At 7:35 AM EST, KDVK was 54°F with a 52°F dew point, south wind near 5 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. At 7:54 AM, KLEX was 57°F with a 51°F dew point, southeast wind near 9 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. No official NWS alert was active for Danville at the final issuance check.

days.label: Tuesday
days.precipitation: 5% or less through late evening; 20–40% after about 1 AM; 70–85% toward daybreak
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Tuesday at issuance. Independent concern is a breezy south-to-southeast wind with gusts around 20–30 mph; rain and isolated thunder approach late tonight.
days.forecast: Mostly sunny, warm and breezy as the pressure gradient tightens ahead of the Plains upper low. The most likely Danville high is near 76°F; the current accuracy summary no longer supports a KDVK high adjustment. South to south-southeast wind runs 8–14 mph with gusts of 20–30 mph. Clouds increase tonight as the low-level jet strengthens. After the verified KDVK low correction, the most likely overnight low is near 60°F. Rain chances rise after about 1 AM and become likely toward daybreak Wednesday.

days.label: Wednesday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Wednesday at issuance. Independent concerns are widespread moderate-to-heavy rain, reduced visibility, brief ponding and south-wind gusts around 25–35 mph; localized shower-related gusts of 40–45 mph are possible. Embedded thunder and a strong storm remain low-probability concerns.
days.forecast: Rain becomes widespread around daybreak, followed by a coherent moderate-to-heavy band through the morning and afternoon. Precipitable water near 1.6–1.75 inches, a deep warm-cloud layer and flow roughly parallel to the front support efficient rainfall and short periods of training. The most likely high is near 69°F. South wind runs 10–18 mph with core gusts of 25–35 mph; a heavier shower may produce a localized 40–45 mph gust. Rainfall should total 1.0–1.75 inches, with a low-probability localized 2–2.5-inch amount. Thunder probability is 10–20%, but weak elevated instability keeps the strong-storm probability low. Rain tapers during the evening, with drizzle possible overnight. After the KDVK low correction, the most likely low is near 51°F.

days.label: Thursday
days.precipitation: 10% or less through evening; 10–20% late Thursday night into early Friday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Thursday at issuance. No threshold independent hazard is expected; the next small cool-shower system remains mainly beyond this forecast window.
days.forecast: Any residual early cloud gives way to mostly sunny or partly cloudy conditions as a transient dry slot crosses the region. The most likely Danville high is near 66°F. Southwest wind runs 3–8 mph with gusts around 10–20 mph. After the KDVK low correction, the most likely overnight low is near 45°F. Clouds may begin increasing late Thursday night, with only a small early-Friday shower risk before this forecast expires.

kentucky.bottomLine: A warm, breezy Tuesday is followed by widespread moderate-to-heavy rain Wednesday. Most places should receive 1.0–1.75 inches, with isolated higher totals and localized 40–45 mph shower gusts possible. Weak instability keeps the broader severe risk low. Thursday is mainly dry before a small late-night or early-Friday shower chance. Most likely Danville highs are 76°F, 69°F and 66°F; bias-corrected lows are 60°F, 51°F and 45°F.
kentucky.confidence: High on Tuesday warmth and Wednesday rain occurrence; moderate-high on the main Wednesday timing and common rainfall range; moderate on localized rainfall maxima, shower-gust coverage and Thursday-night temperatures

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson primary · Central/Pickens County comparison
upstate.summary: Shallow easterly flow and residual Atlantic moisture may regenerate low cloud or patchy fog tonight, but rising heights support a warm, mostly sunny Tuesday. Height falls and increasing southerly moisture transport precede a weakening, occluding front Wednesday. Isentropic ascent and Blue Ridge upslope forcing initiate rain before stronger low-level convergence expands coverage Wednesday afternoon and night. The front brings little cool-air advection; warm, humid air remains beneath cyclonic flow Thursday, allowing terrain-enhanced showers and embedded thunder to continue.
upstate.currentConditions: At 7:54 AM EST, KCEU was 59°F with a 51°F dew point, northeast wind near 6 mph, visibility above 10 miles and broken cloud near 6,000 feet. At 7:55 AM, KLQK was 59°F with a 50°F dew point, east-northeast wind near 8 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. No official NWS alert was active for Clemson or Central. Tempest data was not used.

days.label: Tuesday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Tuesday at issuance. No threshold independent hazard is expected; patchy fog or low stratus may develop after about 4 AM Wednesday.
days.forecast: Mostly sunny and warm as rising heights and daytime mixing overcome shallow easterly moisture. The most likely high is near 74°F. East-northeast wind runs 5–10 mph with gusts around 15–20 mph. Moisture deepens overnight, increasing cloud and producing a conservative patchy-fog risk after about 4 AM. Applying the station corrections, the most likely Clemson low is near 61°F and Central/Pickens is near 57°F.

days.label: Wednesday
days.precipitation: 15–30% early morning; 50–70% late morning and early afternoon; 80–90% late afternoon through night
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Wednesday at issuance. Independent concerns are locally heavy rain, reduced visibility, wet roads and embedded thunder, especially Wednesday evening and night. An isolated strong storm or localized flash-flood problem cannot be ruled out, but organized severe and widespread flooding risks are low.
days.forecast: Patchy fog or low stratus lifts during the morning as isentropic ascent and Blue Ridge upslope forcing begin scattered rain. Coverage expands in the afternoon, followed by the main rain band Wednesday evening and night. The most likely high is near 71°F. East wind runs 2–7 mph with gusts around 10–18 mph. Event rainfall through Thursday morning should total 0.75–1.50 inches, with an isolated amount near 2 inches toward favored slopes. Thunder probability is 25–40%, while the isolated strong-storm probability is near 10–15%. Applying the station corrections, the most likely Clemson low is near 64°F and Central/Pickens is near 60°F.

days.label: Thursday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Thursday at issuance. Independent concerns are scattered heavy downpours, embedded thunder and locally reduced visibility. Organized severe and widespread flooding risks remain low.
days.forecast: The weakening front provides little cool-air advection, leaving the Upstate warm and humid beneath cyclonic flow aloft. Terrain-induced ascent supports renewed scattered showers and embedded thunderstorms through the day, with coverage slowly decreasing Thursday night. The most likely high is near 75°F. Wind is light and variable, becoming south-southwest around 0–5 mph, with gusts around 8–15 mph. Applying the station corrections, the most likely Clemson low is near 58°F and Central/Pickens is near 54°F.

upstate.bottomLine: A warm, mainly dry Tuesday is followed by increasing rain Wednesday and a wet Wednesday night. Scattered showers and embedded thunder continue Thursday because the weakening front brings little cooling. Rainfall through Thursday morning should generally total 0.75–1.50 inches, with a localized amount near 2 inches possible toward favored slopes; later Thursday showers can add to that total. Most likely highs are 74°F, 71°F and 75°F. Bias-corrected Clemson lows are 61°F, 64°F and 58°F, with Central/Pickens near 57°F, 60°F and 54°F.
upstate.confidence: High on Tuesday warmth and dryness; moderate-high on Wednesday-night rain occurrence; moderate on event rainfall amount; lower on exact Wednesday temperature, Thursday shower coverage and embedded-thunder placement

sourceNotes: No official NWS alert was active for the Danville, Clemson or Central point at the final issuance checks. Official NWS alerts remain explicitly separate from this independent analysis.

The latest KDVK, KLEX, KCEU and KLQK observations were dry with clear to broken sky and unrestricted visibility. They support a warm, dry Tuesday and do not independently justify dense-fog language; the Upstate patchy-fog probability is retained because official guidance shows nocturnal moisture return.

The 11:23Z Louisville discussion supports middle-to-upper 70s and gusts near 30 mph today, followed by a 55–65 kt low-level jet, 1.6–1.75-inch precipitable water, training heavy showers and limited elevated instability Wednesday. The 10:58Z Greenville-Spartanburg discussion supports a weakening, occluding front, a west-to-east rainfall gradient and additional cyclonic/terrain-forced showers Thursday.
College of DuPage 12:21–12:25Z radar and infrared imagery showed both forecast regions dry and mostly clear ahead of the organized western cloud and rain shield.

Chris Bailey’s exact November 3 Kentucky Weather Center post, ‘Saying Goodbye to the NAM and Hello to Storms,’ and its NAM animations were consulted as accepted source material. Bailey says the final operational NAM runs bring showers and storms west-to-east tonight and Wednesday, parts of Central Kentucky can receive 1–2 inches, a few strong storms are possible and a smaller cool-shower system may arrive Friday. Details absent from the post or unreadable in its graphics were not inferred. The fresh final NAM cycles remain valid for this forecast, but future updates must not assume new NAM production.

The SPC Day 2 outlook has no severe area and says severe storms are unlikely. This does not materially conflict with Bailey’s conditional few-strong-storm possibility: the forecast retains a low isolated strong-storm risk while rejecting a broader severe episode.

The Danville point forecast gives 77°F Tuesday, 69°F Wednesday and 69°F Thursday. Accuracy-calibrated regional ranges are 74–79°F, 66–70°F and 63–70°F, while prose provides most-likely Danville values of 76°F, 69°F and 66°F. The current accuracy summary supports no KDVK high adjustment and a −2°F KDVK low adjustment.

Fresh KLEX/KSME BUFKIT guidance clusters Tuesday highs in the middle to upper 70s. Complete Wednesday solutions generally support middle to upper 60s to near 70°F and roughly 0.7–1.3 inches, with the final NAM 3-km run a warmer, drier outlier. Wednesday profiles raise precipitable water toward 1.5–1.7 inches and 850-mb wind toward roughly 55–70 mph while keeping CAPE near zero in most solutions.

Upstate official guidance gives 75°F Tuesday, 72°F Wednesday and 76°F Thursday. The calibrated ranges retain the large Wednesday wedge and rain-timing spread while giving most-likely highs of 74°F, 71°F and 75°F.

All 31 GEFS members produce measurable Upstate event rain, 30 exceed 0.25 inch and ten exceed 1 inch; the ensemble mean is 0.86 inch. Deterministic and official event totals span roughly 0.7–1.8 inches, while the final NAM 3-km run is a dry outlier near 0.2 inch. A 0.75–1.50-inch local range preserves the ensemble center and wetter official point guidance.

Fresh KAND and KGSP BUFKIT profiles are regional proxies, not exact KCEU or KLQK profiles. Wednesday instability is generally negligible while precipitable water rises toward roughly 1.5–1.9 inches. A modest conditional CAPE tail develops Wednesday night and Thursday, supporting embedded thunder without implying organized severe convection.

Atmospheric evolution — Central Kentucky: a tightening pressure gradient produces Tuesday warmth and 20–30 mph gusts. Tonight’s 55–65 kt low-level jet rapidly deepens moisture; frontal convergence, a 10,000–12,000-foot warm-cloud layer and boundary-parallel flow then support a coherent, efficient rain band Wednesday. Strong shear is present, but only modest elevated buoyancy limits the broader severe risk. Residual drizzle ends Wednesday night before transient drying Thursday.

Atmospheric evolution — Upstate: shallow easterly moisture may regenerate low cloud or patchy fog tonight. Height falls, southerly moisture transport, isentropic ascent and Blue Ridge upslope forcing expand rain Wednesday. The weakening front provides little cold advection, so warm humid air, cyclonic flow and terrain ascent support renewed scattered showers and embedded thunder Thursday.

The locally extracted seven-model Kentucky package was generated at 2026-11-03T12:59:46Z. All requested model families are represented, normal short-range horizon limits are disclosed and no unavailable period is extrapolated. Its exact-path QPF safety rules are honored; the forecast rainfall range is based only on complete-event sources and the NWS/Kentucky Weather Center synthesis.

KLEX/KSME bracket Danville but are not exact KDVK profiles; KAND is a Clemson-area proxy and KGSP is regional rather than exact KCEU/KLQK guidance. BUFKIT is a profile and visualization interface for underlying models, not an additional independent model. Partial HRRR, RAP, HiResW and NAM 3-km periods were not extrapolated, and BUFKIT surface tables were not used to invent gust forecasts.

The latest cumulative accuracy summary was consulted dynamically from origin/main. It contains 109 verified of 120 checkpoints and all-category accuracy of 79.6% overall, including 83.7% for Central Kentucky and 75.4% for the Upstate.

Current station corrections, empirical lead-specific temperature widths, regime-specific model weights, explicit precipitation and wind windows, measurable wind ranges and official-alert separation were applied. KDVK high is monitoring with no adjustment; applied low corrections are KDVK −2°F, KCEU +2°F and KLQK −3°F.

The low-PoP reliability bin remains underforecast: forecasts averaging 5.7% have observed occurrence of 21.7%. Small overnight and early-Friday shower risks and conditional embedded-thunder risks were therefore retained rather than reflexively suppressed.

Visibility/fog and Upstate weather-regime narrative remain weaker verified categories. Fog probabilities are conservative and observation-based, and Upstate frontal evolution is described probabilistically rather than as a single deterministic outcome.

Temperature cards retain calibrated regional coverage widths, while prose gives narrower most-likely Danville, Clemson and Central values. Overnight ranges represent station and terrain spread, not uncertainty at one exact point.
